newsitem.title: ITALY: FOCUS - Telecom Italia cordless plan stirs things up.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Telecom Italia cordless plan stirs things up.

text.p: An ambitious plan by Italian state telephone company Telecom Italia to launch an advanced cordless phone has jolted Italy's two mobile phone operators and fallen foul of the anti-trust authority.
Telecom Italia last week unveiled plans to invest 1.8 trillion lire ($1.18 billion) in the phone system, to be called Fido, using the Digital European Cordless Telephony (DECT) standard.
The phone would boost the reception of ordinary domestic cordless phones, allowing users to take their telephone with them when they leave home.
Telecom managing director Francesco Chirichigno has said the new service could have one million customers by 1998.

The President of Italy's anti-trust authority Giuliano Amato said that if Telecom Italia went ahead with Fido it would be taking advantage of its dominant position in the fixed-line phone market to compete head on with mobile phone companies.

Amato said that Telecom Italia was effectively offering a mobile phone service. "Technically and juridically it is a mobile telephone service," he told a hearing of the lower chamber of parliament's transport committee on Tuesday.

Amato said the government had not yet regulated cordless telephony but he added: "If the monopolist of fixed line telephony (Telecom Italia) extends itself there (to mobile phones), it extends its own monopoly into a liberalised sector."
Chirichigno hit back on Wednesday. "It has been authorised and we will continue on this path. I fail to see a dominant position," he told reporters after leaving a parliamentary hearing.
A spokesman for the authority said on Wednesday that the body would issue a formal opinion following Amato's remarks.

Italy has two licensed mobile phone operators -- Telecom Italia Mobile (TIM), spun off from Telecom Italia last year, and Omnitel Pronto Italia, a venture controlled by information technology group Olivetti.
TIM and Omnitel are both under pressure as they battle to sign up subscribers to their competing GSM services and the government is expected to license a third operator next year.
TIM had 1.1 million GSM subscribers in mid-October while Omnitel, which only started touting business earlier this year, already had 560,000 by end-September.
Omnitel said in a statement earlier this week that it regarded Fido as a mobile service and called on the authorities to lay down clear guidelines to regulate use of cordless phones.

The top management at TIM, which like Telecom Italia is controlled by state telecoms holding group Stet, is believed to be unnerved by its sister company's cordless venture but has moderated its public statements on the issue.
TIM's Director General Massimo Sarmi has said Stet was examining TIM and Telecom Italia's respective business plans to make sure that they did not conflict with each other.

Industry analysts said they believed the cordless phone was unlikely to take away market share from mobile phone operators because it was less versatile and practically unusable in a moving car or in the open country.
"The DECT phone has very low mobility," said Alberto Rolla, a telecommunications analyst at Milan brokerage Pasfin.

Rolla said a cordless phone venture promoted by British Telecom had been a failure and another low-tier mobile phone service in Britain backed by Hong Kong's Hutchison Whampoa in the early 1990s had also failed to take off.
But Italian newspapers reported that a cordless phone service in Japan had won over three million subscribers. $=1,520
